meta.title: Digital sovereignty
meta.description: What digital sovereignty means for public administration and which risks non-European cloud and AI services entail.

hero.title: Digital sovereignty for public administration
hero.lead: Digitalising public administration requires technology that is both powerful and meets the highest standards of security and independence.

intro: Artificial intelligence is becoming a fixed part of modern administrative processes. Yet many AI services run on non-European clouds — with consequences for data protection, security, and the ability to act.

The Centre for Digital Sovereignty (ZenDiS) has defined clear criteria that a digital solution must meet to offer the highest degree of digital sovereignty. Synaplan was built precisely to these standards.

risksSection.title: Five risks of non-European cloud and AI services
risksSection.lead: ZenDiS describes these risks when using non-European services. With Synaplan they can be substantially reduced — without giving up technical innovation.

risks.title: 1. Extraterritorial legal access
risks.text: Data-protection uncertainty caused by foreign authorities accessing personal data.

risks.title: 2. No control over code and data
risks.text: Limited information security when source code and data are neither inspectable nor controllable.

risks.title: 3. Technological lock-in
risks.text: Inflexibility due to missing exit options and dependence on individual vendors.

risks.title: 4. Uncontrollable costs
risks.text: Rising license fees for cloud-based SaaS models with no spending cap.

risks.title: 5. Externally driven innovation
risks.text: Dependence on the proprietary development cycles of global vendors.

next.title: The open source answer
next.text: Synaplan addresses these risks systematically — through consistent open source development within the European ecosystem.

meta.title: Open source strategy
meta.description: How Synaplan meets the five ZenDiS criteria for digital sovereignty through open source.

hero.title: Sovereignty through open source
hero.lead: Synaplan meets the ZenDiS criteria for digital sovereignty — inspectable, adaptable, and developed in the European community.

intro: The Centre for Digital Sovereignty (ZenDiS) has defined five requirements for a digital solution to offer the highest degree of digital sovereignty. Synaplan meets these criteria.
Here is how we put the strict ZenDiS requirements into practice.

criteriaSection.title: Five criteria — five answers from Synaplan
criteriaSection.lead: Every ZenDiS requirement, translated into a concrete Synaplan promise.

criteria.title: Maximum data protection: lawful and GDPR-compliant
criteria.requirement: Lawful operation without the risk of access by foreign authorities.
criteria.promise: Synaplan can be operated fully GDPR-compliant in your own systems (on-premises) or in a secure, German cloud. Your sensitive administrative data is guaranteed to stay where it belongs — protected from access by third parties or foreign states.

criteria.title: Full freedom: no vendor lock-in
criteria.requirement: Ensuring the ability to switch, to prevent dependence on individual vendors.
criteria.promise: Synaplan relies on open standards. You can migrate data and processes at any time and keep the free choice of your IT service providers. Language models can be switched at any point — chat data, memories, and documents remain in your Synaplan instance.

criteria.title: Absolute sovereignty: full control over your AI system
criteria.requirement: Control and the ability to act — even in the event of outage, blocking, or a change of provider.
criteria.promise: Synaplan is yours. Even if conditions change or external systems fail, your AI solution remains fully operational. At no point are you dependent on the infrastructure of a single vendor.

criteria.title: Trust through transparency: inspectable source code
criteria.requirement: Transparency and traceability of the technology, e.g. through inspectable code.
criteria.promise: No “black box” for public administration: Synaplan's source code is available on public repositories (GitHub, Open CoDE) and how it works is fully traceable. This creates the verifiability the public sector needs.

criteria.title: Future-proof: developed in the European open source community
criteria.requirement: The solution can be adapted and shaped by the community or your own service providers.
criteria.promise: Synaplan grows with your requirements. As part of the European open source ecosystem, you benefit from continuous innovation and can adapt, extend, or have the solution tailored precisely by the IT service providers of your choice at any time.

openSource.conclusion: Synaplan combines state-of-the-art artificial intelligence with the values of digital sovereignty — secure, independent, and transparent.

hero.title: From Outlook to the cluster in your own basement
hero.lead: Sovereignty is not created at a single point, but across the entire technology stack — from the familiar work environment to your own hardware.

intro: Synaplan is not an isolated tool but part of an open ecosystem. The AI can be used where your staff already work — and at the same time run entirely within your own infrastructure.
This keeps the path from the email all the way to the language model consistently in European, sovereign hands.

hero.title: About Synaplan & contact
hero.lead: We support public administration in the digitally sovereign use of AI.

about: Synaplan is an open source AI knowledge platform that combines artificial intelligence with the values of digital sovereignty: data protection, transparency, and independence.

Developed within the European open source ecosystem, Synaplan enables on-premises operation with local models as well as the flexible connection of external language models — depending on protection needs and task.
Synaplan is maintained by metadist and the community and is freely available on public repositories.
contact.founder: Behind Synaplan stands metadist data management GmbH — the company vehicle of founder and internet pioneer <ralf>Ralf Schwöbel</ralf>, who has significantly shaped the German internet since the late 1990s: in government advisory boards as well as in numerous open source projects.
contact.advisor: The German technology executive <nemat>Claudia Nemat</nemat> supports the sovereign software-architecture approach as an advisory board member and shareholder, advocating for a free, open (open source) and stable infrastructure.
